section.heading: 7.2. Trigonometric Integrals
section.paragraph: In this section we use trigonometric identities to integrate certain combinations of trigonometric functions.
section.heading: Integrals of Powers of Sine and Cosine
section.paragraph: We begin by considering integrals in which the integrand is a power of sine, a power of cosine, or a product of these.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: Evaluate $$\int\cos^{3}xdx$$ .

Solution Simply substituting $$u = \cos x$$ isn’t helpful, since then $$du = - \sin xdx$$ . In order to integrate powers of cosine, we would need an extra $$\sin x$$ factor. Similarly, a power of sine would require an extra $$\cos x$$ factor. Thus here we can separate one cosine factor and convert the remaining $$\cos^{2}x$$ factor to an expression involving sine using the identity $$\sin^{2}x + \cos^{2}x = 1$$ :
$$\cos^{3}x = \cos^{2}x \cdot \cos x = {({1 - \sin^{2}x})}\cos x$$
We can then evaluate the integral by substituting $$u = \sin x$$ , so $$du = \cos xdx$$ and

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\cos^{3}x}}dx} = {\int\cos^{2}x \cdot \cos xdx = \int{({1 - \sin^{2}x})}\cos xdx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\cos^{3}x}}dx} = {{\int{({1 - u^{2}})}}du = u - \frac{1}{3}u^{3} + C}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\cos^{3}x}}dx} = {\sin x - \frac{1}{3}\sin^{3}x + C}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: In general, we try to write an integrand involving powers of sine and cosine in a form where we have only one sine factor (and the remainder of the expression in terms of cosine) or only one cosine factor (and the remainder of the expression in terms of sine). The identity $$\sin^{2}x + \cos^{2}x = 1$$ enables us to convert back and forth between even powers of sine and cosine.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Find $${\int{\sin^{5}x}}\cos^{2}xdx$$ .

Solution We could convert $$\cos^{2}x$$ to $$1 - \sin^{2}x$$ , but we would be left with an expression in terms of $$\sin x$$ with no extra $$\cos x$$ factor. Instead, we separate a single sine factor and rewrite the remaining $$\sin^{4}x$$ factor in terms of $$\cos x$$ :
Substituting $$u = \cos x$$ , we have $$du = - \sin xdx$$ and so

section.paragraph: In the preceding examples, an odd power of sine or cosine enabled us to separate a single factor and convert the remaining even power. If the integrand contains even powers of both sine and cosine, this strategy fails. In this case, we can take advantage of the following half-angle identities (see Equations 18b and 18a in Appendix D):
$$\sin^{2}x = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos 2x} \right)$$
and
$$\cos^{2}x = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos 2x} \right)$$

example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}x}}dx$$ .
Solution If we write $$\sin^{2}x = 1 - \cos^{2}x$$ , the integral is no simpler to evaluate. Using the half-angle formula for $$\sin^{2}x$$ , however, we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}x}}dx = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\left( {1 - \cos 2x} \right)}}dx} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}x}}dx}{= \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}\left( {x - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2x} \right)} \right\rbrack_{0}^{\pi}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{0}^{\pi}{\sin^{2}x}}dx}{= \frac{1}{2}\left( {\pi - \frac{1}{2}\sin 2\pi} \right) - \frac{1}{2}\left( {0 - \frac{1}{2}\sin 0} \right) = \frac{1}{2}\pi}} \end{array}$$
Notice that we mentally made the substitution $$u = 2x$$ when integrating $$\cos 2x$$ . Another method for evaluating this integral was given in Exercise 7.1.53.
Example 3 shows that the area of the region shown in Figure 2 is $$\pi \slash 2$$ .

The curve starts at the point (0, 0), rises upwards, falls to the x-axis, and ends at the point (0, pi). The area of the region is shaded.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find $${\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx$$ .

Solution We could evaluate this integral using the reduction formula for $${\int{\sin^{n}x}}dx$$ (Equation 7.1.7) together with Example 3 (as in Exercise 7.1.53), but a better method is to write $$\sin^{4}x = {({\sin^{2}x})}^{2}$$ and use a half-angle formula:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx} = {\int{({\sin^{2}x})}^{2}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx} = {\int\left\lbrack \frac{1}{2}(1 - \cos 2x) \right\rbrack^{2}}dx} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx} = {\frac{1}{4}{\int{\lbrack{1 - 2\cos 2x + \cos^{2}(2x})\rbrack}}dx}} \end{array}$$
Since $$\cos^{2}(2x)$$ occurs, we use the half-angle formula for cosine to write
$$\cos^{2}(2x) = \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {1 + \cos(2 \cdot 2x)}\rbrack = \frac{1}{2}({1 + \cos 4x)} \right.$$
This gives

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx} = {\frac{1}{4}\int\left\lbrack {1 - 2\cos 2x + \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos 4x} \right)} \right\rbrack dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx} = {\frac{1}{4}{\int{\left( {\frac{3}{2} - 2\cos 2x + \frac{1}{2}\cos 4x} \right)}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin^{4}x}}dx} = {\frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{3}{2}x - \sin 2x + \frac{1}{8}\sin 4x} \right) + C}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: To summarize, we list guidelines to follow when evaluating integrals of the form $${\int{\sin^{m}x}}\cos^{n}xdx$$ , where $$m \geqslant 0$$ and $$n \geqslant 0$$ are integers.

note.source_type: Strategy for Evaluating ∫ sin m ⁢ x cos n ⁢ x ⁢ d x
note.title: Strategy for Evaluating ∫ sin m ⁢ x cos n ⁢ x ⁢ d x
note.heading: Strategy for Evaluating ∫ sin m ⁢ x cos n ⁢ x ⁢ d x

list.item: (a) If the power of cosine is odd $$\left( {n = 2k + 1} \right)$$ , save one cosine factor and use $$\cos^{2}x = 1 - \sin^{2}x$$ to express the remaining factors in terms of sine: $$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\sin^{m}x}}\cos^{2k + 1}xdx} = {{\int{\sin^{m}x}}{({\cos^{2}x})}^{k}\cos xdx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin^{m}x}}\cos^{2k + 1}xdx} = {{\int{\sin^{m}x}}{({1 - \sin^{2}x})}^{k}\cos xdx}} \end{array}$$ Then substitute $$u = \sin x$$ . See Example 1.

(b) If the power of sine is odd $$\left( {m = 2k + 1} \right)$$ , save one sine factor and use $$\sin^{2}x = 1 - \cos^{2}x$$ to express the remaining factors in terms of cosine: $$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\sin^{2k + 1}x}}\cos^{n}xdx} = {\int{{({\sin^{2}x})}^{k}\cos^{n}x\sin xdx}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin^{2k + 1}x}}\cos^{n}xdx} = {\int{({1 - \cos^{2}x})}^{k}}\cos^{n}x\sin xdx} \end{array}$$ Then substitute $$u = \cos x$$ . See Example 2. [Note that if the powers of both sine and cosine are odd, either (a) or (b) can be used.]

(c) If the powers of both sine and cosine are even, use the half-angle identities $${\sin^{2}x = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - \cos 2x} \right)} {\cos^{2}x = \frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + \cos 2x} \right)}$$ See Examples 3 and 4. It is sometimes helpful to use the identity $$\sin x\cos x = \frac{1}{2}\sin 2x$$

section.heading: Integrals of Powers of Secant and Tangent
section.paragraph: We use similar reasoning to evaluate integrals of the form $${\int{\tan^{m}x}}\sec^{n}xdx$$ . Because $$({d \slash dx})\tan x = \sec^{2}x$$ , we can separate a $$\sec^{2}x$$ factor and convert the remaining (even) power of secant to an expression involving tangent using the identity $$\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x$$ . Or, since $$\left( {d \slash dx} \right)\sec x = \sec x\tan x$$ , we can separate a $$\sec x\tan x$$ factor and convert the remaining (even) power of tangent to secant.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{4}xdx$$ .

Solution If we separate one $$\sec^{2}x$$ factor, we can express the remaining $$\sec^{2}x$$ factor in terms of tangent using the identity $$\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x$$ . We can then evaluate the integral by substituting $$u = \tan x$$ so that $$du = \sec^{2}xdx$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{4}xdx} = {{\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{2}x\sec^{2}xdx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{4}xdx} = {{\int{\tan^{6}x}}{({1 + \tan^{2}x})}\sec^{2}xdx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{4}xdx} = {{\int{u^{6}}}{({1 + u^{2}})}du = {\int{({u^{6} + u^{8}})}}du}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{6}x}}\sec^{4}xdx} = {\frac{u^{7}}{7} + \frac{u^{9}}{9} + C = \frac{1}{7}\tan^{7}x + \frac{1}{9}\tan^{9}x + C}} \end{array}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find $${\int{\tan^{5}\theta}}\sec^{7}\theta d\theta$$ .

Solution If we separate a $$\sec^{2}\theta$$ factor, as in the preceding example, we are left with a $$\sec^{5}\theta$$ factor, which isn’t easily converted to tangent. However, if we separate a $$\sec\theta\tan\theta$$ factor, we can convert the remaining power of tangent to an expression involving only secant using the identity $$\tan^{2}\theta = \sec^{2}\theta - 1$$ . We can then evaluate the integral by substituting $$u = \sec\theta$$ , so $$du = \sec\theta\tan\theta d\theta$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {{\int{\tan^{4}}}\theta\sec^{6}\theta\sec\theta\tan\theta d\theta}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {{\int{{({\sec^{2}\theta - 1})}^{2}}}\sec^{6}\theta\sec\theta\tan\theta d\theta}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {{\int{{({u^{2} - 1})}^{2}}}u^{6}du}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {\int{({u^{10} - 2u^{8} + u^{6}})}}du} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {\frac{u^{11}}{11} - 2\frac{u^{9}}{9} + \frac{u^{7}}{7} + C}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{5}}}\theta\sec^{7}\theta d\theta} = {\frac{1}{11}\sec^{11}\theta - \frac{2}{9}\sec^{9}\theta + \frac{1}{7}\sec^{7}\theta + C}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: The preceding examples demonstrate strategies for evaluating integrals of the form $${\int{\tan^{m}x}}\sec^{n}xdx$$ for two cases, which we summarize here.

note.title: Strategy for Evaluating ∫ tan m ⁢ x sec n ⁢ x ⁢ d x
note.heading: Strategy for Evaluating ∫ tan m ⁢ x sec n ⁢ x ⁢ d x

list.item: (a) If the power of secant is even $$\left( {n = 2k,k \geqslant 2} \right)$$ , save a factor of $$\sec^{2}x$$ and use $$\sec^{2}x = 1 + \tan^{2}x$$ to express the remaining factors in terms of $$\tan x$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{\tan^{m}x\sec^{2k}xdx}} = {\int{\tan^{m}x{({\sec^{2}x})}^{k - 1}\sec^{2}xdx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\tan^{m}x\sec^{2k}xdx}} = {{\int{\tan^{m}x}}{({1 + \tan^{2}x})}^{k - 1}\sec^{2}xdx}} \end{array}$$ Then substitute $$u = \tan x$$ . See Example 5.

(b) If the power of tangent is odd $$\left( {m = 2k + 1} \right)$$ , save a factor of $${\sec x}{\tan x}$$ and use $$\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1$$ to express the remaining factors in terms of $$\sec x$$ : $$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\tan^{2k + 1}x\sec^{n}x}}dx} = {\int{({\tan^{2}x})}^{k}}\sec^{n - 1}x\sec x\tan xdx} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{2k + 1}x\sec^{n}x}}dx} = {{\int{({\sec^{2}x - 1})}^{k}}\sec^{n - 1}x\sec x\tan xdx}} \end{array}$$ Then substitute $$u = \sec x$$ . See Example 6.

section.paragraph: For other cases, the guidelines are not as clear-cut. We may need to use identities, integration by parts, and occasionally a little ingenuity. We will sometimes need to be able to integrate $$\tan x$$ by using the formula established in (5.5.5):
$$\int\tan xdx = \ln|\sec x| + C$$
We will also need the indefinite integral of secant:
$${\int{\sec xdx = \ln}}\left| {\sec x + \tan x} \right| + C$$
Formula 1 was discovered by James Gregory in 1668. (See his biography in Section 3.4.) Gregory used this formula to solve a problem in constructing nautical tables.
We could verify Formula 1 by differentiating the right side, or as follows. First we multiply numerator and denominator by $$\sec x + \tan x$$ :
$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int\sec xdx} = {\int\sec x\frac{\sec x + \tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int\sec xdx} = {\int\frac{\sec^{2}x + \sec x\tan x}{\sec x + \tan x}dx}} \end{array}$$
If we substitute $$u = \sec x + \tan x$$ , then $$du = {({\sec x\tan x + \sec^{2}x})}dx$$ , so the integral becomes $$\int{\left( {1 \slash u} \right)}du = \ln|u| + C$$ . Thus we have
$$\int\sec xdx = \ln|\sec x + \tan x| + C$$

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: Find $${\int{\tan^{3}x}}dx$$ .
Solution Here only $$\tan x$$ occurs, so we use $$\tan^{2}x = \sec^{2}x - 1$$ to rewrite a $$\tan^{2}x$$ factor in terms of $$\sec^{2}x$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\tan^{3}x}}dx} = {{\int{\tan x}}\tan^{2}xdx = {\int{\tan x}}{({\sec^{2}x - 1})}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{3}x}}dx} = {{\int{\tan x}}\sec^{2}xdx - {\int{\tan x}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\tan^{3}x}}dx} = {\frac{1}{2}\tan^{2}x - \ln\left| {\sec x} \right| + C}} \end{array}$$
In the first integral we mentally substituted $$u = \tan x$$ so that $$du = \sec^{2}xdx$$ .

section.paragraph: If an even power of tangent appears with an odd power of secant, it is helpful to express the integrand completely in terms of $$\sec x$$ . Powers of $$\sec x$$ may require integration by parts, as shown in the following example.

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Find $${\int{\sec^{3}x}}dx$$ .
Solution Here we integrate by parts with
$$\begin{array}{rllrll} u & = & {\sec x} & { dv} & = & {\sec^{2}xdx} \\ {du} & = & {\sec x\tan xdx} & { v} & = & {\tan x} \end{array}$$
Then

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\sec^{3}x}}dx} = {\sec x\tan x} - {{\int{\sec x}}\tan^{2}xdx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sec^{3}x}}dx} = {\sec x\tan x} - {{\int{\sec x}}{({\sec^{2}x - 1})}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sec^{3}x}}dx} = {\sec x\tan x} - {{\int{\sec^{3}x}}dx + {\int{\sec x}}dx}} \end{array}$$
Using Formula 1 and solving for the required integral, we get
$${\int{\sec^{3}x}}dx = \frac{1}{2}\left( {\sec x\tan x + \ln{|{\sec x + \tan x}|}} \right) + C$$

section.paragraph: Integrals such as the one in the preceding example may seem very special but they occur frequently in applications of integration, as we will see in Chapter 8.
Finally, integrals of the form
$$\int\cot^{m}x\csc^{n}xdx$$
can be found in a similar way by using the identity $$1 + \cot^{2}x = \csc^{2}x$$ .
section.heading: Using Product Identities
section.paragraph: The following product identities are useful in evaluating certain trigonometric integrals.
To evaluate the integrals (a) $$\int{\sin mx\cos nxdx}$$ , (b) $$\int{\sin mx\sin nxdx}$$ , or (c) $$\int{\cos mx\cos nxdx}$$ , use the corresponding identity:

$$\begin{array}{llcl} {(a)} & {\sin A\cos B} & = & {\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\sin\left( {A - B} \right) + \sin\left( {A + B} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ {(b)} & {\sin A\sin B} & = & {\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\cos\left( {A - B} \right) - \cos\left( {A + B} \right)} \right\rbrack} \\ {(c)} & {\cos A\cos B} & = & {\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\cos\left( {A - B} \right) + \cos\left( {A + B} \right)} \right\rbrack} \end{array}$$
These product identities are discussed in Appendix D.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Evaluate $${\int{\sin}}4x\cos 5xdx$$ .
Solution This integral could be evaluated using integration by parts, but it’s easier to use the identity in Equation 2(a) as follows:

$$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int{\sin}}4x\cos 5xdx} = {{\int{\frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack {\sin\left( {- x} \right) + \sin 9x} \right\rbrack}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin}}4x\cos 5xdx} = {\frac{1}{2}{\int{\left( {- \sin x + \sin 9x} \right)}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int{\sin}}4x\cos 5xdx} = {\frac{1}{2}\left( {\cos x - \frac{1}{9}\cos 9x} \right) + C}} \end{array}$$
